newsitem.title: Bosnia: Defence minister visits German troops in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Defence minister visits German troops in Bosnia.

text.p: German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe inspected his country's troops serving in the NATO-led peace force in Bosnia on Wednesday as they formally launched their mission.
Ruehe attended a ceremony in the capital Sarajevo in which Major-General Klaus Fruhhaber declared his 2,000 troops ready to assume its duties in the Stabilisation Force (SFOR).
Equipped with armoured personnel carriers and reconnaissance vehicles, the soldiers are the first troops from German combat formations deployed abroad since World War Two.
The presence of German soldiers has so far sparked no angry reaction among the former warring factions despite memories of atrocities committed during the Nazi occupation of Yugoslavia.
Ruehe told reporters he anticipated no problems from Moslem, Croat or Serb armies and expected German soldiers would be treated as other members of the NATO-led contingent.
"I am certain that the German soldiers are being respected by all the parties in the conflict," Ruehe said.
Bosnian Serb authorities often accused Germany of siding with their Croat and Moslem foes during the Yugoslav conflict, but they have stayed mostly silent about this month's deployment.
The troops, drawn from a Franco-German brigade in Germany, will work under French command in the southwest near the town of Mostar, inside Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation.
Although they will be based in the federation, patrolling duties will bring the Germans into Serb-controlled territory as well, NATO officers said.
Before talks with the Bosnian collective presidency, Ruehe said he intended to tell Bosnian political leaders it was up to them to forge a lasting peace and not the NATO-led force.
"Our troops are here and the SFOR troops are here to give a framework for the absence of war, but peace you have to make yourselves among the political leaders here," Ruehe told reporters.
Apart from the 2,000 soldiers serving in Bosnia itself, Germany has contributed another 1,000 airmen, sailors and other troops to the NATO-led force in former Yugoslavia.
About 31,000 troops from the NATO alliance and other countries are policing the Dayton peace agreement in Bosnia in an 18-month mission due to expire in mid-1998.
